# teardown

teardown follows one machine, one page: the visitor sees the thing run, presses a button, and the part doing the work opens up while the gauges around it read the real numbers. Left alone, the page tours itself with a cursor, and any click, drag, wheel, or key hands control over, with 25 seconds of quiet handing it back. The same code records a film of the tour, frame by frame, with a score built on the same timeline, at 60 fps with a synced procedural score. Three worked examples are included: a cross-plane V8 with glass liners driven by crank angle and a firing order of 1-8-4-3-6-5-7-2, a Cessna 337 main landing gear folding on a 0 to 1 stroke (a 201 mm rack turning a 32-tooth pinion of 4 mm module through exactly 180 degrees), and Theo Jansen's Strandbeest with 20 legs on one crankshaft driven by wind. Each machine is built from real dimensions in real units, with one input driving every pose and readout, so nothing on screen can disagree with the motion. Rules that decide whether it works: start from a reference, never from imagination; real numbers from one source; one input drives everything; the part doing the work opens up; light studio with one accent; pick the camera for the mechanism; fix collisions with a number, never by hiding them with the camera. A review loop reads sheets of stills from the current render before any machine is reported as done. Limits as written: pages need a first run of npm install plus a Playwright Chromium install, the video needs ffmpeg...
